Oct 16 : Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez will be available for Sunday's Premier League game at Leeds United after the club accepted his apology for criticising its transfer policy, manager Michael Carrick said. Martinez met Carrick and senior club officials on Thursday, two days after suggesting United needed greater investment to compete at the highest level following their 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid. The centre back later apologised for his remarks and Carrick sought to downplay the episode when he spoke to reporters on Friday. "We've moved on from that. It was one of those things. It's really not a drama for the group," Carrick said.

"The squad have trained really well and they are in good spirits. There is a freshness about the group... "He's part of the squad (for Sunday)." The Argentina international had singled out director of football Jason Wilcox in the post-game interview, saying United needed more signings to compete with their rivals and build a squad capable of challenging in Europe. Martinez made the comments at a difficult time for United, who sit 13th in the Premier League table after winning only one of their opening six matches in their worst start in 40 years. The manager said the club had accepted Martinez's apology. "He's released his statement and realised he made a mistake. That's enough for us to move on with," Carrick said. "I understand the emotion. We ask for passion. There's a way of doing that and that's been acknowledged. But we need to carry that passion in the right way." Carrick, appointed permanently in May after overseeing the club's revival last season, has come under pressure following a poor start to the campaign, but said belief within the dressing room remained intact. "I don't need results. We all need results. It's bigger than me... it's not about any individual player. It's about a football club," Carrick said. "There's a lot of people saying a lot of things. That doesn't mean you know what's going on here. "That doesn't distract us from what we are creating here as a group." United travel to seventh-placed Leeds seeking their first victory in more than a month.

Source: Reuters

FAST

BANGKOK, Oct 16 : The artificial intelligence boom is setting off a global race for money, forcing central bankers to contemplate a future in which interest rates stay higher and governments need to tighten their belts after an era of largesse. From silicon chips and data centres to power grids and telecoms networks, governments and companies are pouring money into projects tied directly or indirectly to AI, adding fuel to the global economy and pushing up borrowing costs. Central bankers from the world's largest economies gathering in Bangkok said the boom was also creating fresh inflation pressures and financial risks, because the investment is arriving long before the productivity gains AI promises. "If you're a central banker...you've got to recognise this as a shock," Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said at the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok. "It's obviously hitting the demand side of the economy before it's going to hit the supply side."

Warsh, who said the US was benefiting from a broadening "surge of investment", warned the transition could be "very bumpy" as investors, companies and policymakers grappled with a technology whose ultimate winners remain unclear. Several of his colleagues from the G20 group of large economies also in the Thai capital said it would only take a slight reassessment of the rosy earnings prospects underpinning AI investments to cause profound market ructions, as a selloff in Asian tech stocks showed this week. STARS BEHIND THE CLOUDS The debate marks a striking shift from the years following the 2008 financial crisis, when policymakers worried about excess global savings and inflation that was persistently too low. Now central bankers increasingly see the opposite problem: too much demand for capital. "There is a global fight for money," ECB policymaker Martins Kazaks told Reuters. "Investment in AI is one of the key factors driving up the cost of money." That pressure is being amplified by governments from the United States to Japan and Germany borrowing heavily for defence, industrial policy and energy projects. For central bankers, the implication is that the level of interest rates needed to keep economies on an even keel, known as R-star, may be rising. "The problem at the moment in calculating the R-star is that the stars are covered by the clouds, and the clouds are so thick," South African Reserve Bank Governor Lesetja Kganyago said. "We know that R-star is higher, but we do not know how high." A higher neutral rate means the same level of interest rate is less restrictive than previously thought. "Maybe rates, on average, will be that little bit higher," said Bank of England Chief Economist Huw Pill. The Bank of Japan has already cited AI-related demand as a factor behind its recent rate increases, arguing that investment-driven price pressures have become broader and more persistent. Economists expect the Bank of England to raise rates at its next meeting on November 5. The ECB and Fed raised rates in September, and markets have priced in another move by them both in December.  NO MORE CHEAP MONEY The prospect of structurally higher borrowing costs poses a challenge for governments that built up large debts during years when interest rates hovered near zero. Sovereign bond yields have risen across the world, and in recent weeks some have reached levels not seen since before the global financial crisis. The euro zone, and notably debt-laden France, was seen as particularly exposed. Much of the AI-driven investment surge is taking place in the United States and, to a lesser extent, Japan and other parts of Asia, with ASML and Siemens among the few clear European winners. Meanwhile, the bloc faces higher energy costs from wars in Iran and Ukraine, compounding inflation pressures and squeezing public finances. "There are particular circumstances that lead to some countries being more affected, France being a case in point," ECB President Christine Lagarde said at a CNN event in Bangkok. "And for that one, the primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies."

(Additional reporting by David Milliken and David Lawder; Editing by John Mair and)

Source: Reuters

Oct 16 : New York has barely stopped celebrating its first NBA title in 53 years, and the Knicks are already chasing a repeat in a league that is built to stop one. The NBA has crowned a record eight different champions in the last eight seasons. Rules that make it tougher to stack a roster with superstars have turned the league into a free-for-all. The Knicks, however, have a big edge: the band is back together. New York returns its five best players, Jalen Brunson, Josh Hart, Mikal Bridges, OG Anunoby and Karl-Anthony Towns, along with the chemistry that carried it to the title. THE LEBRON PLOT TWIST

The offseason's biggest story was where the NBA's all-time leading scorer, LeBron James, would land after splitting with the Los Angeles Lakers. The surprise winner of the sweepstakes was the Philadelphia 76ers. James admitted he would have liked to play for the Knicks, but said that door closed once they won the title. So the 41-year-old will take his talents to Philadelphia instead of the Big Apple, although he will reportedly be living part-time in New York and commuting by helicopter. There he joins Jaylen Brown, who was stunningly traded by the Celtics in the offseason, along with Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and VJ Edgecombe. The question is whether the pieces fit, since all five players are accustomed to having the ball in their hands. "They are like a room that has five beautiful couches in it," ESPN's Brian Windhorst told ABS-CBN News. "But you don't need five couches in a room. You need a couch and a chair, a table, a TV and a mirror, and that's going to be a challenge. Can they all fit, or do you have to put one couch up along the wall." WELCOME TO THE GARDEN James could hardly have a more dramatic debut. The four-time champion opens his Philadelphia career at Madison Square Garden on Tuesday, just after the Knicks raise their championship banner. His teams have often started slowly in his first season with them. If that happens again, Philadelphia's famously impatient fans may not wait long to let everyone know how they feel. The payoff could be historic. A title in his record-extending 24th season would make James the first player to win championships with four different teams. EVERYONE ELSE WANTS IN The rest of the league has its own plans when the 2026-27 season tips off on Tuesday: • Victor Wembanyama and the San Antonio Spurs want revenge after a bitter Finals loss. • Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and the Oklahoma City Thunder are going for a second title in three years. • Stephen Curry leads a Golden State Warriors team trying to revive its title hopes.

Source: Reuters

FAST

BANGKOK, Oct 16 : The head of the IMF on Friday appealed to global leaders to cooperate in the face of multiple economic risks, including rapid advances in AI and a prolonged war in the Middle East, as Washington hailed what it sees as US-led economic momentum. Their contrasting views echoed throughout this year's annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok, as finance officials and central bankers from around the world took stock of a global economy rocked by high inflation and rising interest rates that have kept growth sluggish and increased inequality. The IMF on Tuesday slightly raised its global growth forecast to 3.1 per cent in 2026, well below the historical average, as it flagged significant growth and financial stability risks from a potential ending of the AI investment boom, growing debt levels and the ongoing Middle East conflict. Absent the US-Israeli-led war against Iran and Tehran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz that triggered a massive global energy shock, the IMF has said it would have expected AI to have fueled much stronger growth.

On Friday, IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva said the sheer speed of technological change added to the long list of challenges, including disruptions to the global trading system, high food and energy prices and lingering wars, all of which threatened to widen the gulf between advanced economies and the world's poor. Bond markets, she said, were clearly sensing the risks, with US, German and Japanese 10-year sovereign yields reaching their highest levels in decades. "The need of the hour is for urgent and practical international cooperation," Georgieva, the first IMF chief from an emerging market economy, said at a plenary session on Friday. She told a subsequent panel that she spent sleepless nights worrying about how to regulate AI and ensure that poorer countries weren't left behind by its breakneck-speed development. US Treasury Under Secretary Erin Browne, in a call with reporters, pushed back against those warnings, hailing record highs on the US stock market, strong US economic output and improvements in Japan's economy. "The IMF needs to take a more balanced approach to assessing the global economic outlook," she said, adding: "The global economy has demonstrated significant resilience with strong US growth helping to support broader economic and financial stability." She said that the Fund should give equal consideration to "opportunities for positive economic shocks, particularly those driven by American innovation and super intelligence, energy abundance, and productivity-enhancing reforms." US President Donald Trump's policies on tax, trade, energy and deregulation were paving the way for stronger investment, higher productivity and durable economic growth, she said. AI JITTERS HIT STOCKS Emerging market stocks have been volatile in recent weeks, roiled by expectations of higher US interest rates that have sent borrowing costs sharply higher. Major markets have also been hit by the growing concerns over the AI investment cycle. South Korean shares posted their biggest weekly fall in 18 years as investors questioned the sustainability of the AI boom, while Japan's stock market lost 5.4 per cent over the week. Eli Remolona, governor of the Philippines' Bangko Sentral ng Pilipanas, said in an IMF panel discussion earlier in the week that he was concerned Asia had not learned the lessons of its destructive financial crisis in the late 1990s. Before the Asian financial crisis broke out in 1997, economies drew huge capital inflows that prompted the World Bank to describe it as the "East Asian miracle," Remolona said. "Investment poured into Asia, and then you had the crisis because it wasn't really a miracle. I think we have to remind ourselves about that. We have to guard against that kind of crisis," he said on Wednesday. "We have not really been making a lot of effort looking at that kind of crisis." Illustrating the vulnerability to sudden shifts, Indonesian stocks fell 11.6 per cent on Friday, their steepest one-day fall in 28 years, after global index provider MSCI said the Indonesian market was no longer worthy of "emerging market" status. Officials at the IMF and World Bank this week said they are seeing elevated demand for grant and loan programs. IMF strategy chief Christian Mummsen said the IMF's low-interest lending to low-income countries had quadrupled since the COVID pandemic, and demand was expected to remain strong. About 60 per cent of the IMF's financing since COVID had gone to low-income countries, he said.  Developing countries are increasingly outspoken about their concerns. Barbados this week joined a group of countries calling for the creation of an international panel to address inequality, citing geopolitical tensions, climate change and rapid technological advances that could further divide wealthy and poorer nations.

Source: Reuters

FAST

AMSTERDAM, Oct 16 : Websites and online delivery services at grocery chains belonging to Dutch supermarket operator Ahold remained offline for a fifth day on Friday following what the company has described as a "cybersecurity incident" that prompted it to shut down some of its own IT systems.  An Ahold spokesperson said the parent company cannot comment about the situation at its individual chains. Its US brands, which include Stop & Shop, Giant Food, Hannaford and Food Lion, are collectively one of the largest food retailers in the United States. Physical stores remain open.  Ahold's Albert Heijn chain, the Netherlands' largest, has been gradually recovering from the shutdown that began October 11, disrupting its distribution centres and leading to empty produce shelves. Albert Heijn does not expect online delivery to resume before Sunday. The Netherlands' Justice Minister David van Weel called on the company on Friday to file a criminal complaint over the incident, which Ahold has avoided describing as a hack, saying in a statement that no "customer, associate and partner data was taken".

CAPE TOWN, Oct 16 : A player from South Africa’s Lions rugby team died on Friday at the team's hotel in France, the day before the club are due to make their debut in the European Champions Cup away at La Rochelle. The identity of the player has not been announced while the team contacts his family in South Africa, SA Rugby officials told Reuters on Friday. French media reports said the player was found unconscious in a shower cubicle at a hotel on the Ile de Re in France, where the team had been staying since Tuesday. Emergency services were called shortly after 10 a.m. and attended to the player, who was in cardiorespiratory arrest. Attempts to resuscitate him were unsuccessful, the reports added.

FAST

Oct 16 : Australia fast bowler Josh Hazlewood predicts reverse swing may be crucial to the outcome of the three-test series against South Africa, where abrasive pitches are helping revive a fading art. Hazlewood extracted swing and used the reversing ball to good effect in the first test at Kingsmead in Durban, which ended on Tuesday with Australia winning by 214 runs. Reverse swing could be as vital for the second test in Gqeberha, which starts on Sunday and where the St George's Park wickets are expected to be similar. The art of reverse swing has faded in recent years with greener wickets and lusher outfields keeping the ball newer and less likely to rough up.

“The ball still looks new late in the innings if it gets that far,” said Hazlewood about playing back home in Australia, but it is a different story on tour in South Africa. “It’s abrasive wickets. It's very hard underfoot,” he explained. "We probably got a hint of swing in the first innings and then as the game goes it just deteriorates more and you get a bit more. So we knew it was crucial," he said of their success in Durban, where he returned carer-best figure of 6-49 in the last innings to secure Australia’s triumph. "If the wicket is hard, firm, deteriorating and not much seam movement, you're probably going to get that reverse swing," Hazlewood told a pitch-side press conference on Friday as Australia prepared for Sunday. "You probably want the ball a bit harder and a little bit of reverse swing rather than a lot of reverse swing and the ball's soft. That's much easier to navigate as a batsman,” he added. Hazlewood, now 35, produced his performance in Durban after missing all of last season's Ashes series through injury. “I just play every test match that comes,” he said of his longevity. "Could be your last one whenever. I don’t think about it much. "I think you know it was great fun last week playing with the same guys. Doing the work in the last innings and taking the 20 wickets for the game on what was a pretty flat wicket for the majority. I don’t look too far ahead these days.”

Oct 16 : South Africa will seek to show their heady ascent to the top of the test cricket pile was no accident as they bid to level the series against Australia in the second test, starting on Sunday in Gqeberha. The hosts suffered a 214-run defeat to Australia in the first test that ended in Durban on Tuesday, a setback that left their status as world test champions looking increasingly fragile. South Africa secured a dramatic five-wicket victory over Australia to win the World Test Championship last year at Lord’s in London, but their qualification for the final prompted debate. They played fewer tests than the likes of England and India and faced what was widely regarded as an easier schedule in the qualifying period.

Their winning form leading up to the WTC final also masked some poor batting performances, which coach Shukri Conrad acknowledged finally caught up with them against Australia at Kingsmead, where they looked anything but world champions. “We’ve been heavily reliant on (captain) Temba (Bavuma) and (opener) Aiden Markram and then the lower order runs,” he said after Australia exposed their batting fragility. Several changes are expected for the second test where Matthew Breetzke is set to be given a renewed chance to open alongside Markram. Ryan Rickelton is primed to take over as wicketkeeper from Kyle Verreynne but move down the order. Tristan Stubbs, who batted at number five for the first test, has been omitted, which could open the door for Marques Ackerman to make his test debut. RABADA BACK AFTER LENGTHY ABSENCE South Africa will welcome back paceman Kagiso Rabada for his first outing since the Indian Premier League in May, placing considerable expectation on his shoulders despite his lengthy absence. That means they will drop one spinner. Australia’s selection is also keenly anticipated but with Cameron Green’s return from injury likely delayed, they might resist the temptation to make any changes after such an emphatic win. One possibility, however, is that Scott Boland is brought into the attack as Australia monitor the workloads of Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc after all three bowled at least 29 overs in the first test. Persistent rain and damp conditions are forecast for Gqeberha, particularly on the opening two days, which raises the prospect of delays or a shortened match at St George’s Park.

Tokyo, Oct 16 : The next phase of Japanese corporate reform took center stage at the Sohn Conference in Tokyo, as hedge fund managers highlighted investment opportunities ranging from a financial conglomerate's capital allocation strategy to an X-ray scattering firm's AI solutions. At the inaugural Sohn Conference in Japan, which invited 14 funds to pitch their top investment ideas, more than half of the investors favored the theme of corporate reform. Daisuke Nakayama, a portfolio manager at Hong Kong-headquartered Polymer Capital, picked Orix Corporation, a financial services firm, saying the change in management marks "a big turning point" for the company's transformation into a global investment firm. "The new leadership has a greater focus on capital allocation and ROE," Nakayama said, adding the firm is now using overseas capital, including from Qatar Investment Authority, to bid for companies.

The number of activist campaigns in Japan hit a record last year, according to brokerage Jefferies, after years of pressure from regulators and the Tokyo Stock Exchange on companies to improve shareholder returns and invest in growth.  BEYOND DIVIDENDS AND BUYBACKS Fund managers said that the next chapter is not just about companies increasing dividends and buybacks but also about focusing on those deploying capital to expand businesses and drive long-term growth. One example is Rigaku, an X-ray equipment supplier pivoting to semiconductor metrology, measuring and inspecting chips.  New York-based Indus Capital Partners said it had invested in the company and had engaged with the firm to sell a stake to a US semiconductor firm to drive revenue.  As semiconductor companies are going into vertical structures to scale, X-ray is needed to detect defects deeper in the 3D chips, said Byron Gill, managing partner at Indus. Rigaku might be one of the few companies that "has the key to unlocking scale for the semiconductor industry in the middle of a super cycle", he added, forecasting a 100 per cent rise in its valuation by 2029. REFORM THEME DOMINATES The corporate reform theme still has a long way to run, market participants said.  "Japan changes slowly, but once the change starts, it does not reverse," said Naohide Une, partner and CEO at Investment Lab, a former senior managing director at Japan Post Bank. He picked Japanese chemical company Ube Corporation for its corporate reform efforts. In a separate Q&A session, Seth Fischer, founder of activist Oasis Management, said his fund may substantially increase its stake in Japanese electric motor maker Nidec. AI AS A BACK-OFFICE TAILWIND AI was another key investment theme.  Investment firms Ruane Cunniff and Japan Catalyst picked software companies Money Forward and OBIC Business Consultants, respectively.  They argued that back-office software operators are AI winners rather than losers, as clients require accuracy. And these businesses are helping Japan overcome labor tightness, they said.

Oct 16 : Spain have been fined $20,000 and ordered to partially close their stadium for their next friendly after supporters chanted Islamophobic slogans twice during a game against Egypt in March, FIFA said in a statement. The sanctions relate to incidents at the RCDE Stadium near Barcelona, home of LaLiga club Espanyol, where some Spain fans chanted, "Who doesn't jump is a Muslim" during a World Cup warm-up match which ended in a 0-0 draw. After the second occurrence of the chant, the stadium announcer issued a warning and the scoreboard displayed a message against discriminatory behaviour. Spain winger Lamine Yamal, who is Muslim, condemned the chants at the time, describing them as disrespectful and intolerable and calling those responsible "ignorant and racist".

Spanish police launched an investigation the following day while world governing body FIFA later started disciplinary proceedings against the Spanish soccer federation (RFEF). The RFEF argued that the word 'Muslim' was "neither insulting nor pejorative", adding the fans' conduct should be assessed under FIFA's Article 17, which covers political, ideological, religious or offensive messages, rather than Article 15, which deals with discrimination and racist abuse. However, FIFA's disciplinary committee rejected that argument, saying Article 15 does not require the explicit use of a slur and that a term can be discriminatory when used in context as "an insult, taunt, or marker of inferiority". FIFA fined the RFEF and ordered the closure of at least 15 per cent of available seats for Spain's next friendly. Reuters has contacted the RFEF for comment.

Oct 16 : Michael Saylor's Strategy faces potential removal from MSCI's global equity indexes under new rules adopted on Thursday, threatening billions of dollars in passive investment in the bitcoin buyer. Shares of Strategy, the world's biggest corporate bitcoin holder and a constituent of the MSCI USA and MSCI World indexes, fell 2.7 per cent in premarket trading on Friday. MSCI said on Thursday non-operating companies will be ineligible for its Global Investable Market Indexes from the close of November 30, as part of its November index review. It will publish the final list of affected companies on November 11. The decision follows a review MSCI began a year ago, when it proposed excluding digital asset treasury companies on the grounds that they resemble investment funds, which are already barred from its indexes. MSCI deferred that plan in January and opened a broader review on all non-operating companies.

MSCI defines non-operating companies as investment funds and business development companies, and other companies whose finances make them look like one. Strategy and Japan's Metaplanet are on MSCI's list of potential deletions. SharpLink and several other crypto treasury companies are on a watchlist for possible removal. The changes are aimed at expanding MSCI’s exclusions for passive investment vehicles, with companies required to meet financial tests on their operating assets to remain eligible. Index inclusion matters to companies such as Strategy because passive funds and other investors tracking benchmarks are required to hold their shares.  Strategy did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment outside business hours. The company warned last year that an exclusion would result in $2.8 billion of its stock being liquidated and would "chill" the industry. Strategy, which pioneered the model of raising money through stock and debt sales to buy bitcoin, had a market value of about $64.3 billion at Thursday’s close. PARIS, Oct 16 : European stocks rose on Friday as markets stabilised after a sharp tech-led selloff, while the dollar headed for a weekly loss. Markets have been rattled this week by concerns over higher interest rates and the debt-fuelled financing behind the AI boom, triggering a selloff in technology and chip stocks. Traders increased bets on further US rate hikes after stronger-than-expected inflation data on Wednesday, while investors piled into Treasuries and other government bonds. Asian stocks mostly rose and bond markets steadied on Friday, with investors reversing some of the previous session's moves.

Indonesian equities suffered their biggest drop since 1998 after index provider MSCI said the country's market no longer merited emerging market status and outlined plans to remove it from key indexes tracked by funds.  Turkey's main stock index also slid more than 3 per cent after MSCI froze certain changes to its Turkey equity indexes.     At 1055 GMT, the MSCI World Equity Index was up 0.4 per cent but still set for a weekly loss. European stock indexes, hit less hard by Thursday's selloff, were higher, with the STOXX 600 up 0.6 per cent, Germany's DAX up around 1 per cent and France's CAC 40 up 0.5 per cent. London's FTSE 100 was up less than 0.1 per cent. US stock futures also pointed to a recovery on Wall Street, with S&P 500 futures up 0.2 per cent, although Nasdaq futures were still in the red as investors remained worried about mounting credit risks linked to the AI trade, particularly among heavily indebted data-centre operators such as CoreWeave, which helped trigger Thursday's selloff. "The question of monetization to me is still the big question that is not fully answered. There are still some doubts about the sustainability of the profits and the margins from some actors in the sector," said Amelie Derambure, a senior multi-asset portfolio manager at Amundi in Paris. Still, Derambure said she remained overweight US equities and expected earnings to be strong enough to limit any market correction. DOLLAR FALLS, BONDS RECOVER The dollar fell 0.4 per cent, leaving the dollar index at 101.65 and on track for its first weekly decline after three weeks of gains, as lower Treasury yields reduced the currency's appeal. Further worries about AI would push the dollar down further, analysts said. The weaker dollar helped lift the euro from its recent 17-month low. It was last up 0.4 per cent at $1.1257. European government bond yields edged higher on Friday, with Germany's 10-year yield at 3.4355 per cent. Even so, yields remained lower on the week as investors sought the safety of government debt amid concerns about AI-related companies' finances. G7 government bond markets were on course for their strongest weekly performance since late May. The correlation between German bond yields and the STOXX 600 turned positive this week for the first time since August, suggesting government debt is regaining some of its safe-haven appeal. That relationship weakened this year amid concerns that the war in Iran could fuel inflation and keep borrowing costs higher for longer. Oil prices were mixed, with Brent crude futures at $106.14 a barrel but still headed for a weekly gain amid concerns over Middle East supplies. Attacks around the Strait of Hormuz have surged in the past 10 days. Gold gained support from the weaker dollar, rising to about $4,174.52 an ounce.

Source: Reuters

Oct 16 : Rafael Jodar apologised on Friday for swearing at a ball kid during his last-16 match at the Shanghai Masters, with the Spaniard saying that he could not control his emotions when frustrations boiled over. After losing a point in Wednesday's win over Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp, Jodar angrily asked the ball kid to hand him his towel, swearing in Spanish. The chair umpire Jimmy Pinoargote, who also speaks Spanish, gave Jodar a code violation for unsportsmanlike conduct. Pinoargote then warned Jodar not to speak like that to ball kids when the 20-year-old argued with him over the violation. "I shouldn't have done that to the ball kid. It was my mistake. I respect a lot the ball kids and the umpires in all the matches and all the tournaments. I shouldn't have treated the ball kid the way I did," Jodar told reporters after his quarter-final win over Casper Ruud.
